titre: Callendar, 1938: a steam technologist calculates the warming
accroche: In 1938, an engineer calculates 0.003 °C of warming per year and finds 0.005 in the thermometer records. Simpson sees more of a coincidence.
contenu_vulgarise:
On February 16, 1938, the Royal Meteorological Society hears a paper signed by a man who is not a meteorologist. G. S. Callendar presents himself as a “steam technologist” at the British Electrical and Allied Industries Research Association. His manuscript, received on May 19, 1937, opens with an observation: few specialists in the heat exchanges of the atmosphere would admit that human activity could influence it on this scale. He sets out to show that this influence is not only possible, but already at work.

## Three measurements put end to end

Callendar proceeds in three stages. First the gas. In fifty years, combustion has added to the air about 150,000 million metric tons of carbon dioxide, and he estimates that about three quarters of it has stayed there. The ocean contains about sixty times more than the atmosphere, but absorbs it slowly: Callendar assigns it an equilibrium time of two to five thousand years. For the period from 1900 to 1936, he calculates a rise close to 6%.

Then the heat. From the absorption coefficients of carbon dioxide and water vapor, he calculates the radiation that the atmosphere sends back toward the ground, and deduces from it a warming of 0.003 °C per year at the current rate.

Finally the thermometer. According to the paper's abstract, records from 200 stations show that the world's temperature has risen, on average, by 0.005 °C per year over the past half-century. The world curve drawn in the body of the text (figure 4) rests, for its part, on 147 records: the abstract and the detail do not give the same count. Callendar left the Arctic stations out of this curve, because their rise is much stronger.

The calculation gives 0.003, the measurement 0.005: same sign, same order of magnitude.

## What the room objects

The paper is printed with the discussion that followed it, and it is that discussion that matters here. Sir George Simpson praises excellent work, then attacks the method. The atmosphere is not in radiative equilibrium, he says: its temperature is set almost entirely by the vertical movements of the air, so the effect of a single factor cannot be calculated. As for the simultaneous rise in carbon dioxide and temperatures, he judges it more likely coincidental.

C. E. P. Brooks notes that the rise is about ten times stronger in the Arctic than in the middle or low latitudes, and does not believe that a change in carbon dioxide could produce such a gap. J. H. Coste doubts that thermometers from thirty years ago allow reasoning about fractions of a degree, and that the old carbon dioxide measurements are comparable to the new ones.

Callendar answers point by point. He admits that temperature control is complex, but maintains that a substance that retards the transfer of heat must produce a rise in the regions farthest from space. He agrees that the Arctic rise is too strong to come from carbon dioxide alone.

## An agreement is not a proof

1938 is sometimes summed up in one sentence: Callendar was right, nobody listened. The record of the session says otherwise. He was listened to, and the objections were precise: they concerned what the calculation left out. Spencer Weart, a historian at the American Institute of Physics, also notes that Callendar estimated the effect of a doubling of carbon dioxide at 2 °C, on grounds he considers fragile.

The agreement between 0.003 and 0.005 therefore does not say that the method was complete. It says that a calculation, of which Arrhenius had given a first version as early as 1896, was being confronted with thermometers, and that the room could contest each step.

These objections are printed after the article. Which of them have been resolved since, and by what measurements?

repere.texte: In the abstract of his 1938 paper, Callendar estimates at 150,000 million metric tons the carbon dioxide added to the air by combustion in fifty years, of which about three quarters would have stayed there. He calculates a warming of 0.003 °C per year, and finds 0.005 °C per year on average across 200 weather stations. In the body of the paper, his world curve rests on 147 records.
repere.source: G. S. Callendar, “The artificial production of carbon dioxide and its influence on temperature,” Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society, vol. 64, 1938, p. 223 (abstract)

carte.punch: 1938: a steam engineer puts a number on warming from CO₂.
carte.idee: In 1938, Callendar calculates a warming of 0.003 °C per year due to carbon dioxide, and finds 0.005 in the temperature records. Simpson, present at the session, judges the method incomplete and the rise more likely coincidental.

quiz.question: What is Simpson's main objection to Callendar's 1938 calculation?
choix: The atmosphere's temperature is set by the vertical movements of the air, not by radiation alone
The 1900 carbon dioxide measurements are too imprecise to be compared with recent ones
Callendar used too few weather stations to establish a world average
Carbon dioxide does not absorb infrared radiation at the wavelengths where the Earth emits
quiz.explication: Simpson objects that the atmosphere is not in radiative equilibrium: its temperature depends almost entirely on the vertical movements of the air. The imprecision of the old measurements is Coste's objection, the number of stations is not at issue, and the infrared absorption of carbon dioxide is not disputed.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was G. S. Callendar's profession, the author of the 1938 paper?
choix: Arctic climatologist who had measured the polar stations himself
Meteorologist by training, employed by the Royal Meteorological Society
Steam technologist at the British Electrical and Allied Industries Research Association
Physicist specializing in infrared radiation at Cambridge
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Callendar presents himself as a steam technologist at the British Electrical and Allied Industries Research Association, and not as a meteorologist, physicist or climatologist.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What objection does C. E. P. Brooks raise against Callendar's calculation?
choix: The absorption coefficients of carbon dioxide are poorly measured in the laboratory
The Arctic rise is ten times stronger than elsewhere, a gap that carbon dioxide alone does not explain
The ocean absorbs carbon dioxide faster than Callendar estimates in his calculation
The weather stations used are poorly distributed over the globe's surface
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Brooks notes that the temperature rise is about ten times stronger in the Arctic than in the middle or low latitudes, a gap that, in his view, a change in carbon dioxide alone cannot produce.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the comparison between the abstract of Callendar's paper and its body text (figure 4, table VIII) reveal?
choix: The abstract announces 200 stations, but the figure and table in the body text rest on 147, Arctic excluded
The abstract and the body text give exactly the same number of stations, 147
The body text uses more stations than the abstract, 220 versus 200
The abstract mentions no number of stations, only the body text gives one
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The paper's abstract (p. 223) announces 200 stations, but figure 4 and table VIII, in the body text, rest on 147 records, the Arctic stations being excluded from this curve.
